title: Diamond quantum-sensing platform with integrated boron-doped diamond microwave antenna and thermometer
authors: Masahiro Ohkuma, Ryo Matsumoto, Shintaro Adachi, Shinobu Onoda, Kensei Terashima, Takao Watanabe, Yoshihiko Takano, Keigo Arai
abstract: Wide-field nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetic imaging at cryogenic temperatures requires microwave excitation and reliable knowledge of the temperature near the sensing region. Here, we report an integrated diamond quantum-sensing platform combining an ensemble of NV centers with a boron-doped diamond (BDD) microwave antenna and thermometer formed on the same diamond substrate. The BDD antenna provides microwave excitation for optically detected magnetic resonance measurements, and the BDD thermometer monitors the thermal environment near the NV sensing region. The BDD thermometer detected laser-induced local heating that was not clearly resolved by a stage-mounted thermometer. Using this platform, we imaged the temperature-dependent Meissner response of multiple cuprate superconductors while recording the temperature. These results demonstrate that the integrated BDD--NV platform provides a practical approach for cryogenic wide-field magnetic imaging with integrated microwave delivery and local thermometry.
summary: This work reports an integrated diamond platform combining NV centers for magnetic sensing with BDD structures for microwave delivery and local thermometry. By demonstrating that the integrated BDD thermometer accurately measures local heating effects missed by external thermometers, the authors prove this platform is a practical tool for quantitative, wide-field magnetic imaging of temperature-sensitive materials like superconductors at cryogenic temperatures.
main_problem: Wide-field nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetic imaging at cryogenic temperatures requires both microwave excitation and accurate local temperature knowledge near the sensing region.
main_result: The integrated boron-doped diamond (BDD)–NV platform successfully enables wide-field magnetic imaging while simultaneously providing local thermometry, demonstrating its practicality for cryogenic quantum sensing.
method: The authors integrated NV centers, a BDD microwave antenna, and a BDD thermometer onto a single diamond substrate to perform Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR) measurements.
model_or_system: The system utilizes NV centers in diamond for magnetic sensing, coupled with BDD structures for microwave delivery and local temperature monitoring. This integrated platform allows for simultaneous measurement of magnetic fields and thermal environment near superconducting samples.
key_observables: Temperature-dependent Meissner response of cuprate superconductors, magnetic-field maps, and local temperature readings (comparing BDD vs. stage thermometer).
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures, microwave power, superconducting transition temperatures (Tc), and local heating effects (e.g., laser-induced heating > 4 K).
main_assumptions: The BDD thermometer's resistance-to-temperature calibration required fitting data with a fourth-order polynomial, and the microwave power was estimated based on nominal input power.
figures_summary: Figures show the platform schematic, comparisons of temperature readings (BDD vs. stage thermometer) under varying power, and temperature-dependent wide-field ODMR imaging of superconducting samples.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the need for integrated sensing, details the platform construction (NV/BDD), presents comparative measurements showing the BDD thermometer's superior local temperature resolution, and concludes by applying the platform to map superconducting properties as a function of local temperature.
why_interesting: The development of an integrated, on-chip platform for quantum sensing that self-monitors its local thermal environment is crucial for quantitative studies of quantum materials under extreme conditions, bridging quantum sensing with advanced metrology.

Figure 1f shows the temperature dependence of the electrical resistance of the BDD thermometer. The re- sistance exhibited a non-monotonic temperature depen- dence, with a minimum at approximately 220 K. To de- termine the temperature from the BDD resistance in the range relevant to the present measurements, the data be- tween 10 and 120 K were fitted with a fourth-order poly- nomial. The resulting fitting curve was used to convert the measured resistance into temperature.
